 Business News OPINION Columns MCA21 at 20: Filing extensions cannot become the new normal MCA21 at 20: Filing extensions cannot become the new normal
 Two decades after MCA21 began, recurring deadline extensions expose the need for a more reliable filing system, clearer rules and greater accountability.
 Advertisement Share: 
 Financial statements are generally due within 30 days of a company's annual general meeting (AGM), and annual returns within 60 days. Dr. Ranjith Krishnan and A Sekar Oct 30, 2026,
 Updated Oct 30, 2026 2:51 PM IST
 Subscribe to Notifications On 24 October 2026, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) gave companies more time to submit their annual filings for 2025-26. Financial statements, filed through Form AOC-4 and related forms, may now be submitted until 31 December 2026, and annual returns, filed through Forms MGT-7 and MGT-7A, until 31 January 2027, without additional late fees. The relief is welcome. Yet a basic question remains: why must companies and professionals wait until near the end of the filing season to learn whether another extension is coming? 
 Advertisement Read More India's online corporate filing system, MCA21, began in 2006. The published circular record shows no comparable general relaxation for ordinary annual filings for the financial years 2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24; relief returned for 2024-25 and 2025-26. Did companies file more promptly during the three years without extensions? Did the website perform better? Without actual filing data, we cannot answer these questions. The presence or absence of a circular tells us little about the causes of delay. 
 The Companies Act, 2013 sets a clear sequence. Financial statements are generally due within 30 days of a company's annual general meeting (AGM), and annual returns within 60 days. The latest circular waives additional fees during specified periods but does not extend the AGM deadline. These filings are not private exchanges between companies and the Government: banks, investors and suppliers rely on them. Even accurate financial information loses some of its value when it reaches the public months late. 
 Advertisement ALSO READ |  ITR filing 2026: NBFC, HFC interest income must be reported separately — what it means  
 Not all delays have the same cause. One company may have incomplete accounts; another may have completed its work but repeatedly failed to upload a form because of website errors. A blanket extension helps both, while giving little recognition to those who met the original deadline. The Ministry should distinguish genuine system failures from delays attributable to companies and provide a clear route to relief where a system failure can be demonstrated. 
 The Delhi High Court addressed a related issue in Luckygirl Fashion Private Limited v. Union of India in July 2025. Interpreting a 2019 extension, it held that additional fees for companies filing after the extended date could be charged from the end of that period, not the original due date.
 Advertisement The 2026 circular expressly provides a different basis: a company that misses the relaxed deadline faces fees calculated from its original due date. The earlier ruling cannot be applied mechanically to the new wording. Companies should nevertheless know the financial consequences before relying on an extension. A simple worked example would help. 
 MUST READ |  GST changes from November 1, 2026: Refunds, return filing and ITC rules explained 
 A related issue emerges from the Institute of Company Secretaries of India's (ICSI) October representation seeking more time. It referred to the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) granting 21 additional days for certain tax-audit reports and income-tax returns. Professionals understandably face overlapping deadlines. But the comparison raises a harder question: were the accounts ready before the AGM deadline, and had shareholders adopted them?
 The extension request does not tell us. Preparation, approval and filing are distinct obligations. That distinction should guide any reform. The Companies Act permits financial statements that have not been adopted at an AGM to be filed in accordance with the prescribed procedure.
 Income-tax returns follow a separate statutory timetable. Any proposal to require companies to file Form AOC-4 before submitting their income-tax returns therefore deserves careful examination. Such a requirement would need a clear legal basis and safeguards for situations in which the adoption of financial statements or electronic filing is delayed.
 Advertisement DON'T MISS |  ITR filing deadline for corporates extended to November 21 
 A measured link between the two systems, through integrated filing, nevertheless deserves consideration. Until then, corporate income-tax returns could ask for the MCA filing acknowledgement number where financial statements have already been filed, or a declaration that the MCA filing is pending. After studying the results, the Government could consider aligning the relevant deadlines or, following the necessary legal changes, requiring specified companies to file with the MCA first, subject to appropriate exceptions. This approach would make the status of corporate accounts visible without automatically turning an MCA filing delay into an income-tax default. 
 Meanwhile, avoidable filing problems should be addressed directly. The Ministry could announce exceptional relief earlier, record attempted submissions during verified website outages and publish simple instructions when forms change. It should also report how many companies met the original deadline and how many needed the extension. These figures would help establish whether annual concessions address genuine difficulties or merely postpone the rush. 
 Twenty years after MCA21 began, success should be measured by whether companies prepare their accounts on time and the public receives them promptly. A dependable filing system would make extensions the exception, not an annual expectation. Nobody should have to wait for a circular to rescue the calendar.  
  Dr. Ranjith Krishnan is Associate Professor, Christ University, Delhi NCR. Mr. A. Sekar is Practicing Company Secretary, Mumbai. Views are personal
